preamble: Unrounding combined with lowering of the high front rounded vowel [y(ː)], the i-mutation product of *u(ː), to [e(ː)]. It is the hallmark of Kentish and south-eastern English. Elsewhere Old English y and ȳ either stayed rounded (south-west, West Midlands) or unrounded to [i(ː)] (north, East Midlands). In Kentish, /y(ː)/ and /ø(ː)/ had already been replaced by /e(ː)/ by the late 9th to early 10th century, and the change survives in Middle Kentish spellings such as ver 'fire', velle 'fill' and bregge 'bridge'.

examples.note: The long vowel ȳ > ē. Initial voicing f- > v- is a separate south-eastern feature.
Short y > e. This is the south-eastern type, against Midland and Northern fillen.
Listed as a late Kentish alternative form of Old English cyning.
The Kentish, East Anglian and East Saxon form, against Southern and West Midland brugge and Midland brigge.
